name: nSuns

card.summary: A high-volume, weekly-progression variant of Jim Wendler's 5/3/1 lifting program that people run to build strength and muscle mass for a bigger, more muscular physique.
card.note: Very high weekly volume; descriptions of the program say recovery, food intake and conservative starting weights matter.

quick.overview:
nSuns is a strength-training template created by a Reddit lifter who posts as nSuns. It takes Jim Wendler's 5/3/1 percentage system and adds many more sets per session, with progression decided every week by how many reps the lifter gets on a final top set. Lifters use it to add strength on the squat, bench press, deadlift and overhead press, which in turn is a route to more muscle on the chest, back, shoulders and legs.

The program circulates through Reddit's lifting communities and through fitness-app and spreadsheet sites. It has not been tested in published trials, so what is known about it comes from the program's descriptions and from lifters' own logs.
quick.how: Lifters pick a 4-, 5- or 6-day version, set a training max as a percentage of their best lift, and follow a spreadsheet or app that calculates the weights. Each day has a main lift with roughly nine working sets ending in a top set taken to as many reps as possible, followed by a second lift for about eight sets at lower percentages and some accessory work. Guides describe it as a block of several months and recommend eating in a surplus.
quick.risks: Descriptions from program hosts say the volume is high and that it can burn lifters out faster than standard 5/3/1, particularly if they start with a training max set too high or sleep and eat too little. They describe it as aimed at lifters past the beginner stage. As with any heavy barbell program, technique and load selection affect injury risk.

lead: nSuns, also written nSuns 5/3/1 or nSuns LP, is a high-volume strength-training program adapted from Jim Wendler's 5/3/1 system by a Reddit user who posts as nSuns [1][2]. It keeps Wendler's use of a training max and percentage-based sets, but adds many more working sets per session and increases weights every week rather than every cycle [1][2].

People use programs like this to get stronger on the four big barbell lifts (squat, bench press, deadlift and overhead press). Gaining strength is one way lifters build the muscle that shapes a fuller chest, wider shoulders, thicker back and stronger legs, and the program's high set counts are what followers cite for size as well as strength [1][2].
The program is shared mainly as spreadsheets and through training apps. No published trial has examined nSuns specifically.

chain: Higher weekly volume on squat, bench, deadlift and press
Faster strength progression driven by weekly top sets
More training stimulus for muscle growth
angle.text: nSuns is a training template for getting stronger on compound lifts. Lifters who follow it, usually while eating in a calorie surplus, report using it to add size as well as strength, which changes how their physique looks.

paras: The program is built on percentages of a training max, set at about 90 percent of a lifter's one-rep max [1][2]. Each session pairs a main lift with a second, supplementary lift. Program hosts describe about nine working sets on the main lift, ending in a top set taken to as many reps as possible, followed by about eight sets on the second lift [1][2]. Across both lifts a session can reach around 17 working sets before accessories [2].
Versions run four, five or six days per week, with squat-focused and deadlift-focused six-day variants also circulating [1]. Each of the four main lifts is trained two to three times per week [2].

Jim Wendler's 5/3/1 is a percentage-based system built around the squat, bench press, deadlift and overhead press, usually one per day. In the version summarised on a community fitness wiki, weekly main work uses sets of five, three, then a 5/3/1 pattern, with the last set of each session taken for as many reps as possible, and with supplemental and assistance exercises added by the lifter [3].

nSuns keeps that percentage logic but compresses it. Boostcamp describes the style as Wendler in the front and Sheiko, a high-volume Russian powerlifting method, in the back [2]. Where standard 5/3/1 raises the training max after a cycle, nSuns adjusts weights weekly, depending on how many reps the top set produces [1].

In one hosted description, no increase follows a top set of zero or one rep, and larger jumps follow higher rep counts, with the largest increases after six or more reps [1]. If lifters stall, the program describes resetting the training max by about 10 percent [2].

sections.h: Who it is described as suiting
paras: Program hosts describe nSuns as suited to late-novice and early-intermediate lifters who recover well and want high volume, not to complete beginners, who they say progress on simpler linear programs [1]. Boostcamp specifies lifters with at least a year of consistent training [2]. Both suggest starting with the 4-day version and adding days only if recovery allows [1][2].

Program descriptions flag the high volume as the main caution: weekly progression can lead to earlier stalls, and burnout comes faster than with slower programs [1][2]. They recommend a conservative starting training max, running the program in a calorie surplus rather than during a diet, and treating it as a block of several months [2].

No studies found. Research on resistance training in general has examined how training volume and frequency relate to muscle growth, but no trial has tested nSuns or compared it with other 5/3/1 variants.
